report:
I wouldn’t answer a flat “no.” The better evidence-based answer is: **not proven; possible small benefit, but low-certainty**. A 2023 RCT meta-analysis found magnesium improved depression scores, but it included only **7 trials/325 adults**, with differing doses/forms and likely heterogeneity—enough to signal benefit, not settle efficacy: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychiatry/articles/10.3389/fpsyt.2023.1333261/full  

The best-known trial (126 adults, mild–moderate depression) reported symptom improvement, but its design limits confidence as definitive proof: https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0180067  

Observational data link higher dietary magnesium with lower depression risk, but mostly cross-sectional studies cannot show that supplementation treats depression: https://academic.oup.com/nutritionreviews/article-abstract/83/2/217/7685053  

Practical takeaway: correcting low magnesium is reasonable; magnesium is generally safe at recommended intakes, though excess can cause diarrhea and kidney disease raises risk: https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/Magnesium-HealthProfessional/ It should not replace standard depression care.
